waves.title: What a new UK stadium costs to build in 2026
waves.keywords: stadium construction cost UK, cost to build a stadium, cost per seat stadium, arena construction cost UK, stadium cost by capacity
waves.brief:
Reader: a club chief executive, venue owner, council regeneration lead or consultant at feasibility stage, deciding whether to redevelop or build new and what number to put to a board. They want a defensible cost per seat range and why real projects miss it.

What ranks now and why it fails: Wikipedia and StadiumDB give one headline figure per venue with no scope definition, fan sites recycle club releases, and TheStadiumBusiness reports each announcement without aggregating or reconciling them. None explains that a construction contract value and a total project cost are different numbers, which is why one stadium is quoted at wildly different prices. That reconciliation is the whole article.

Structure: (1) headline range per seat, flagged as our arithmetic and not a published figure. (2) A comparison table. (3) Why the figures disagree, scope by scope. (4) The cost drivers: groundworks and remediation, structural span, premium fit-out, inflation between approval and completion. (5) New build versus redevelopment.

SOURCE ANCHORS, all checked live 17 Nov 2026. Manchester United confirmed plans on 11 March 2025 for a 100,000-capacity stadium at around 2 billion pounds, with chief executive Omar Berrada saying that figure also covers fan zones and a megastore, and Sir Jim Ratcliffe saying refurbishment would have cost about 70 per cent of a new build (club announcement, via StadiumDB and Sportcal, 11 March 2025). Everton's Bramley-Moore Dock stadium, design capacity 52,888, was fixed with Laing O'Rourke at a 500 million pound construction price (Place North West, 2022), while later reporting put total project spend at 760 to 800 million pounds, a different scope covering land, dock infill, enabling works and finance. Co-op Live: Oak View Group chief executive Tim Leiweke is quoted saying it passed 400 million pounds and that OVG, City Football Group and contractor BAM would spend close to 450 million privately; capacity 23,500 standing and 20,500 all-seated; opened 14 May 2024. Liverpool's Anfield Road End was approved at about 60 million pounds (Construction Enquirer) and later reported at about 80 million for roughly 7,000 extra seats.

NOTES FOR THE WRITER, and these are not optional. The frequently quoted 365 million pound 2022 estimate for Co-op Live traces back to a Wikipedia infobox in the research behind this brief. Do not print it without a primary source; if you cannot find one, use the Leiweke quotes, which are attributable, and say the earlier estimate is unverified. The final Anfield Road End outturn and the Fulham Riverside Stand figure were not verified either: source both from primary documents or leave them out. Every figure names its source in the same sentence.

STRUCTURAL: use 'stadium construction cost UK' in the first paragraph. The comparison must be a table: venue, capacity, scope of the figure, figure, source, date. Link out to Place North West and the club announcements.

Scope limits: business and construction only. No match reports, results, transfers or team news, ever. No betting or gambling promotion; a betting-branded venue may be named as plain fact.

waves.title: What stadium naming rights are actually worth
waves.keywords: stadium naming rights value, how much are naming rights worth, naming rights deal structure, arena naming rights UK, stadium sponsorship value
waves.brief:
Reader: a commercial director or venue owner about to take a naming right to market, or a brand being pitched one, deciding what to ask or pay and over what term. They need an annual market range, the valuation method, and the clauses that decide whether a deal is worth its headline.

What ranks now and why it fails: the results are listicles of the biggest deals ever, mostly US and undated, mixing total value with annual value so a ten-year deal looks ten times bigger than it is. SportsPro and Sportcal report signings well but without method and behind a paywall; Wikipedia lists sponsor names with no values. None of them says the thing that matters most: most UK club deals are undisclosed, so published figures are estimates.

Structure: (1) the range per year, not per contract. (2) How a valuation is built. (3) A comparables table. (4) Deal structure: term, activation and signage obligations, category exclusivity, renaming costs, relegation clauses, termination on brand damage. (5) Why a venue might stay unnamed.

SOURCE ANCHORS, checked live 17 Nov 2026. The Sponsor's European Stadium Naming Rights Fair Market Sponsorship Value Report, published 27 January 2026 and valued as at 19 December 2025 using market regression benchmarking under IVS 105: the Santiago Bernabeu tops it at 21.1 million euros (18.4 million pounds) a year with no naming partner; a built New Trafford is put at 17.2 million euros (15 million pounds) a year, or 172 million euros over ten years; the top 75 European stadiums combine to 520 million euros; Cardiff's Principality Stadium sits 5.1 million euros (4.5 million pounds) a year below fair value; Allianz Stadium in Turin is 3.3 million euros above. Everton announced Hill Dickinson in May 2025 with terms undisclosed, calling it one of Europe's largest; the Guardian's Andy Hunter put it near 10 million pounds a year, other reporting nearer 6 million, with neither party confirming. Co-op signed 15 years on the Manchester arena, reportedly 125 million dollars (Pollstar, 25 September 2020). O2's ten-year North Greenwich deal is reported at 155.9 million dollars (fcbusiness).

DO NOT USE WITHOUT RESOLVING: Arsenal's renewed Emirates arrangement is reported at 70 million pounds, but the sources do not say whether that is annual or total, and it bundles front-of-shirt sponsorship. Either verify it or state plainly that it is unresolved. Never silently pick one reading.

STRUCTURAL: use 'stadium naming rights value' in the first paragraph. The table must separate annual from total value and flag every undisclosed deal as estimated. Link out to The Sponsor's report page and the announcements cited.

Scope limits: no match reports, results, transfers or team news, ever. A betting sponsor may appear as plain fact, never as promotion, with no betting link, offer or odds.

waves.title: How a venue is licensed to hold a crowd
waves.keywords: stadium safety certificate, safe capacity calculation, Green Guide sports grounds, P and S factors, sports ground safety certificate
waves.brief:
Reader: a safety officer, venue general manager or safety advisory group member who needs to know why their certificated capacity is below their seat count, and what would change it.

What ranks now and why it fails: the SGSA's own site is the authority but splits the method across short pages that omit the numbers and point back to the Green Guide. Legislation.gov.uk gives the statute with no operational explanation, and law firm notes cover liability rather than the capacity arithmetic. Nobody puts the method and the arithmetic on one page.

Structure: (1) who issues what: the local authority issues the certificate under the Safety of Sports Grounds Act 1975, and the SGSA licenses grounds under the Football Spectators Act 1989. (2) The four calculations. (3) The (P) and (S) factors. (4) What changes a capacity. (5) Licensed standing. (6) A certificate review checklist.

SOURCE ANCHORS, checked live 17 Nov 2026 on sgsa.org.uk. The SGSA states that final capacity is the lowest of entry, holding, exit and emergency exit capacity, that in no circumstances should a larger number be admitted, and that safe capacity is not the number of seats or standing spaces available. Seated holding capacity is seats minus any unusable through seriously restricted views or poor condition. Exit capacity must be based on the narrowest point, a vomitory or staircase, not the exit gate. Holding capacity is then adjusted by the (P) factor for physical condition and the (S) factor for safety management, each from 0.0 to 1.0, with the lower governing; the Green Guide sets no fixed values, with indicative questions in Annex A and Annex B. The current edition is the 6th; the SGSA's own page says the 7th is due Spring 2029. Licensed standing began 1 January 2022 with five early adopters against 16 criteria, including barriers in home and away sections and a seat or space per person; SI 2022/728 widened it in July 2022, and CFE Research's July 2023 evaluation found a negative impact on ambulant disabled supporters.

NOT VERIFIED, so do not invent them: entry and exit rates per minute, standing density per 10 square metres, and evacuation times sit in Green Guide chapter 2, not on the SGSA web pages. Take them from the Guide itself, citing edition and chapter, or omit them.

STRUCTURAL: use 'stadium safety certificate' in the first paragraph. The four calculations must be a table: the limb, what it measures, what constrains it, what a venue can do about it. Link out to the SGSA safe capacity, P and S factors and licensed standing pages.

Scope limits: no match reports, results, transfers or team news, ever. No betting or gambling promotion.

waves.title: Premium hospitality: what a seat really yields
waves.keywords: stadium hospitality revenue, premium seat yield, matchday revenue per seat, stadium hospitality yield, premium seating business case
waves.brief:
Reader: a commercial or hospitality director building next season's premium inventory, or a project sponsor deciding how many premium seats go into a new stand and at what price. The decision is how much of a capacity increase to give to premium, and what yield justifies the fit-out and the general admission seats displaced.

What ranks now and why it fails: the top results are hospitality resellers, so every number is a retail price with no yield, cost or occupancy behind it. Deloitte's Annual Review is authoritative but reports at league level, never per seat, and club accounts do not disclose hospitality separately. The arithmetic nobody publishes is the article.

Structure: (1) the market picture. (2) The arithmetic: yield per seat per event times events a year, less cost of sale, staffing and food cost, which is exactly what resellers' prices hide. (3) A disclosed-revenue table. (4) What drives yield: event count, term length, catering inclusion, pitchside access, renewals. (5) The risks: cannibalising general admission, and overbuilding into a weak corporate catchment.

SOURCE ANCHORS, checked live 17 Nov 2026. Deloitte's 35th Annual Review of Football Finance, covering 2024/25, reports Premier League matchday revenue passing 1 billion pounds for the first time, up 133 million or 15 per cent, inside total revenue of 6.8 billion pounds, up 8 per cent. Tottenham's 2024/25 figures show record matchday revenue of 126.5 million pounds against 105.8 million on 1.7 million paying attendance, inside record total revenue of 565.3 million, with matchday at 22 per cent of revenue against commercial's 49 per cent. On 2024/25 matchday revenue Manchester United led at 160 million pounds, Arsenal 154 million, Tottenham 126 million. Arsenal's 2026/27 premium packages run from 2,995 pounds a head for lower-profile fixtures to 6,999 pounds against other top clubs (City AM, 2026).

NOTE FOR THE WRITER: the Tottenham figures come from published analysis of the accounts rather than the filed accounts themselves. Confirm them at Companies House before publishing. TWO NUMBERS ARE BANNED FROM THIS PIECE: there is no published Premier League figure for hospitality as a share of revenue, and the claim that the top 5 per cent of premium seats produce 40 per cent of venue revenue is US-centric and unsourced. Do not reach for either.

STRUCTURAL: use 'stadium hospitality revenue' in the first paragraph. The club comparison must be a table: club, matchday revenue, season, source, and any derived per-attendee figure flagged as derived. Any yield per seat must be arithmetic from disclosed revenue and capacity, labelled as ours. Link out to the Deloitte review and Companies House.

Scope limits: no match reports, results, transfers or team news, ever. No betting or gambling promotion, and no hospitality package with a betting element.
